amendments.rule: The definite direct-object marker `אֵת` (H853) has no English realization of its own and is normally its own `unrepresented` unit; that is the ruling on the large majority of its occurrences. It takes English only where the ASV spends a word on the object relation itself and no other morpheme licenses that word. Four families qualify. An English verb may reach its object through a preposition — *hearken unto*, *spake unto*, *inquire of*, *fight against*, *send for* — where that preposition exists only to attach the object to the verb; it is the marker's rendering, not the object noun's, and the marker heads on it. An appositional or resumptive marker may be rendered *even* or *to wit*. **But only a marker standing on the very phrase that English word introduces.** Where the ASV writes an appositional *even* or *to wit* before a phrase no marker marks, no morpheme licenses it and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, whatever markers stand elsewhere in the clause: `וְחַקּוֹתָ עָלֶיהָ עִיר אֵת־יְרוּשָׁלִָם` → *portray upon it a city,* ***even*** *Jerusalem* gives *even* to the marker, which stands on the appositive itself, while `נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֵת־שְׁנֵי עֲוֺנָם לְמִסְפַר יָמִים שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵאוֹת וְתִשְׁעִים יוֹם` → *a number of days,* ***even*** *three hundred and ninety days* leaves the *even* `added`, because the clause's one marker stands on `שְׁנֵי עֲוֺנָם`, which the ASV renders bare. Do not reach across the clause for a marker to carry such a word, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. **But an *even* the ASV writes inside another morpheme's own multi-word rendering is not an appositional *even* at all, and the preceding sentence does not reach it.** Where the ASV expands an extent or limit preposition as *even unto*, *even to*, *even till* or *even for*, the whole expression is that preposition's rendering and belongs to its unit, headed by rule 24 on the word carrying the relation — *unto*, *to*, *till*, *for* — and the *even* is neither `added` nor any marker's, whatever markers stand elsewhere in the clause: `וַיִּירַשׁ אֶת־אַרְצוֹ מֵאַרְנֹן עַד־יַבֹּק עַד־בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן` → *from the Arnon unto the Jabbok* ***even unto*** *the children of Ammon* gives *even unto* to the second `עַד`, which is the morpheme the two words are written for. Read what the English word stands before, which is this rule's subtraction test again: an appositional *even* stands before a nominal that renames what precedes it, and this one stands before the object of the very preposition written beside it, so dropping it diminishes that preposition's rendering and nothing else. Two limits. Where a connective morpheme stands in the clause and the ASV writes a bare *even* for it, rule 14 governs and the word is the connective's; the corpus aligns a waw to *even* in 179 units and to *even unto* in none, so read which of the two the ASV has written. And where the ASV leaves the preposition's own relation unstated, rule 40 governs as before and there is no expression to place. The corpus aligns a preposition to *even unto* in 33 units and `עַד` to *even to* in 28 more, always headed on the second word. **Read that first limit as a count of the ASV's words against the morphemes standing in the phrase, and not as a test of whether the word *even* stands alone on the page.** Where a conjunction morpheme stands immediately before the limit preposition and the ASV writes *even unto*, *even to*, *even till* or *even for* at the head of that phrase, two English words answer to two morphemes and neither is a surplus: the waw takes the *even*, exactly as rule 14 gives the *even* of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea* to the waw written there, and the preposition takes the relational word alone, exactly as it does when the same phrase is written *and unto*. `וְעַד־בַּעַל גָּד` → ***even unto*** *Baal gad* divides that way, and it divides identically to the `וְעַד` of `וְעַד מִשְׂרְפוֹת מַיִם` → ***and unto*** *Misrephoth maim* standing in the same chapter, the waw taking whichever connective the ASV wrote for it and the `עַד` taking *unto* in either case. Count the phrase's connective morphemes against the ASV's connectives and read which pair of members each stands between, as rule 26 counts a `מִן … עַד` range's connectives and rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; a waw beside such an expansion takes the bare *even* and never the pair, which is what the corpus's count of no waw aligned to *even unto* records. The whole-expression reading of the preceding sentences governs where no connective morpheme stands beside the preposition, which is what `עַד־יַבֹּק עַד־בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן` above is, and it governs a comparative or other preposition expanded the same way with no conjunction in the phrase: `כַּחוֹל` → ***even as*** *the sand* keeps both words with the `כְּ`. So read whether a conjunction is present before placing the *even*, exactly as rule 14's own closing sentences direct for a coordinator and rule 51 for an *also*. And a marker on an object the ASV fronts before its clause and resumes inside it with a pronoun may be rendered *as for*: `וְאֶת־הַיְבוּסִי יוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם לֹא־יָכְלוּ בְנֵי־יְהוּדָה לְהוֹרִישָׁם` → *And* ***as for*** *the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out* gives *as for* to the marker, headed on *as* by rule 24, since the resuming *them* is the suffix's under rule 18 and nothing else answers to the two words. **The same limit governs that third family.** Where the ASV writes *as for* before a fronted phrase no marker stands on, no morpheme licenses the expression and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, headed on *as*: `וּמַרְאֵיהֶם דְּמוּת אֶחָד לְאַרְבַּעְתָם` → *And* ***as for*** *their appearance, they four had one likeness* leaves the *as for* `added`, because `מַרְאֵיהֶם` is a bare noun and suffix with no marker and no preposition on it. Do not fold the expression into the fronted noun to avoid the `added`, for the reason just given about a surplus *even*, and do not reach for rule 33: that rule gives a supplied function word to a noun whose own case-function licenses it, and a topicalized nominal's fronting is not such a case-function. Where a morpheme does stand on the fronted phrase it takes the expression, whether that morpheme is a marker as above or a fronting `לְ` — `לָאוֹפַנִּים לָהֶם קוֹרָא` → ***As for*** *the wheels, they were called* gives *As for* to the `לְ` under rule 11. **And a marker on a direct object the ASV demotes to a role phrase takes the preposition written for it.** Where the ASV recasts the marked object as the role the thing serves and writes a supplied *for* or *as* before it, promoting the object's appositive to the English verb's object — `וְהֵבִיא אֵת־קָרְבָּנוֹ שְׂעִיר עִזִּים` → *he shall bring* ***for*** *his oblation a goat* — that word is the marker's and it heads on it, since the marked noun keeps its own English and nothing else in the clause answers for the preposition. Rule 33 is what governs the same clause written without a marker, and it says so in its own terms: a nominal with no preposition and no object marker on it takes the supplied word itself, as `וְהֵבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ` → ***for*** *his oblation* and `יָבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ` → ***as*** *his oblation* do. So read whether a marker stands on the noun before placing the word, and do not leave it `added`: one of the two morphemes always licenses it. Test by subtraction: drop the English word and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If nothing but the object relation is diminished, the marker takes the word; if the ASV writes the object bare — *he built the house* — the marker is `unrepresented`. Do not confuse H853 with its homograph the preposition `אֵת` *with* (H854), which is an ordinary preposition aligning by rule 11.
amendments.why: JOS.11.17 (`וְעַד־בַּעַל גָּד` → *even unto Baal gad*) met a case rule 16 had not considered, and the rule as written pointed the wrong way. Its *even unto* paragraph sends the whole expansion to the limit preposition, and its first limit tells a reader to 'read which of the two the ASV has written' — which, read straight, gives *even unto* whole to `עַד` and leaves the waw `unrepresented`. But rule 14 already aligns the waw of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea* to the *even*, and the corpus figure rule 16 itself cites (a waw to *even* in 179 units, to *even unto* in none) is evidence for the split rather than against it. The chapter decides it: `וְעַד` is rendered *and unto* twice at 11.8 and *even unto* once at 11.17, in the same list of limits, and reading the first two as waw-plus-preposition and the third as preposition-alone would make one construction two. The amendment states the count the rule was already gesturing at — connective morphemes against the ASV's connectives, as rules 26 and 42 count — and keeps the whole-expression reading for a phrase with no conjunction in it, which is what rule 16's own `עַד־יַבֹּק` example is and what JOS.11.4's `כַּחוֹל` → *even as* is. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule because the misleading sentence is inside rule 16 and would otherwise stay there for whoever reads it first.

conventions: הַר: rendered 'hill country' at 11.2, 11.3, 11.16 and 11.21, each unit headed on 'hill' because 'country' is the supplied generic and 'hill' is what loses the lexeme when dropped (rule 31); rendered 'mount' before a name at 11.17 (mount Halak, mount Hermon), where the article standing on it is unrepresented because the ASV writes no 'the', and הַר חֶרְמוֹן is rendered attributively under rule 28 rather than with an 'of'. Read what the ASV wrote before applying either.

לְפִי־חֶרֶב → 'with the edge of the sword' is split three ways at 11.11, 11.12 and 11.14: לְ takes 'with', פֶּה takes 'the edge' with its supplied determiner, and חֶרֶב takes 'of the sword' with its own. Rule 30's fusion of לְפִי does not reach it, because the ASV spends a word on each morpheme and rule 2 splits wherever ownership is independently recoverable.

'even' beside a limit preposition: where a conjunction morpheme stands, the waw takes the 'even' and the preposition takes the relational word alone, so וְעַד־בַּעַל גָּד → 'even unto Baal gad' at 11.17 divides exactly as וְעַד מִשְׂרְפוֹת מַיִם → 'and unto Misrephoth maim' does twice at 11.8, the waw taking whichever connective the ASV wrote. Where no conjunction stands, the whole expansion is the preposition's: כַּחוֹל → 'even as the sand' at 11.4 keeps both words on the כְּ. See the amendment to rule 16.

בֵּלֶת is the morpheme the ASV's negative realizes wherever it writes one, whatever preposition it stands on: 'none' at 11.8 after עַד, which keeps only 'until', and 'no' at 11.20 after the privative לְ, which keeps only the complementizer 'that' (rules 15, 48). Where the ASV instead writes the exceptive 'save', as at 11.19, the particle takes that word and there is no negation to place.

Do not confuse H853 with its homograph the preposition `אֵת` *with* (H854), which is an ordinary preposition aligning by rule 11.
amended.why: JOS.11.17 (`וְעַד־בַּעַל גָּד` → *even unto Baal gad*) met a case rule 16 had not considered, and the rule as written pointed the wrong way. Its *even unto* paragraph sends the whole expansion to the limit preposition, and its first limit tells a reader to 'read which of the two the ASV has written' — which, read straight, gives *even unto* whole to `עַד` and leaves the waw `unrepresented`. But rule 14 already aligns the waw of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea* to the *even*, and the corpus figure rule 16 itself cites (a waw to *even* in 179 units, to *even unto* in none) is evidence for the split rather than against it. The chapter decides it: `וְעַד` is rendered *and unto* twice at 11.8 and *even unto* once at 11.17, in the same list of limits, and reading the first two as waw-plus-preposition and the third as preposition-alone would make one construction two. The amendment states the count the rule was already gesturing at — connective morphemes against the ASV's connectives, as rules 26 and 42 count — and keeps the whole-expression reading for a phrase with no conjunction in it, which is what rule 16's own `עַד־יַבֹּק` example is and what JOS.11.4's `כַּחוֹל` → *even as* is. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule because the misleading sentence is inside rule 16 and would otherwise stay there for whoever reads it first.

report: Checked all 53 candidate lemma groups plus the six `added` units the candidate table is blind to. No cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

כָּל + לֹא is fused to one English word at 11.11 (none), 11.13 (none) and 11.15 (nothing), and split at 11.14 (neither ... any). That is rule 35's own condition applied in both directions — one word carrying both senses fuses, a word written for each splits — not one construction analysed twice.

כָּל־מַלְכֵיהֶם is the same three morphemes at 11.12 and 11.17 and is analysed two ways, because the ASV wrote 'all the kings of them' in the first and 'all their kings' in the second. The suffix takes 'of them' where the ASV writes the partitive and 'their' where it writes the possessive (rule 18); the construct takes a supplied 'the' only in the first, since an English possessive already determines the phrase in the second (rule 29). Licensed by the translation.

הַר is 'hill country' at 11.2, 11.3, 11.16 and 11.21, headed on 'hill' by rule 31's subtraction, and 'mount' before a name at 11.17, where rule 28 governs מוּnt Hermon and the article goes unrepresented because no 'the' is written. Licensed by the translation. Likewise בֵּלֶת: 'none' at 11.8, 'save' at 11.19, 'no' at 11.20, the negation-bearing analysis uniform wherever the ASV writes a negative.

The six `added` units were checked against the temptation to fold, since the table cannot see them. Every object pronoun with a suffix behind it goes to that suffix (11.6, 11.12, 11.14, 11.17, 11.21) and the two with none — 'thereof' at 11.1, 'them' at 11.11 — are `added` under rule 44; every English 'and' with a waw behind it goes to the waw, and the one asyndetic coordination, at 11.12, is `added` under rule 14. Consistent in both directions.

One edge a later reader may contest, left as the verse pass had it: the supplied 'to' opening 11.3, whose governing אֶל stands in 11.2. Rule 10 forbids reaching into the neighbouring verse, and rule 33 does not reach a list member whose relation is an elided preposition rather than a case-function, so `added` stands.

BSB disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. The 20 Td cases are the determiner count of rules 41 and 47, where a demonstrative or כֹּל standing in the phrase takes the one written determiner; the two אֵת are rule 16's ordinary ruling; the three לְ (11.8, 11.9, 11.20) are rule 40, and 11.20 is rule 43's express instruction that a written הָיָה takes the 'have' itself and leaves its preposition nothing; the הִיא at 11.10 is rule 20's tripartite clause, where the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and the copula joins the predicate. No accepted edge was changed to improve the aggregate.

One amendment returned, to rule 16. JOS.11.17 met a real conflict in the contract: rule 16 sends 'even unto' whole to the limit preposition, while rule 14 gives the 'even' of וָיָמָּה → 'even unto the sea' to the waw. The chapter settles it — וְעַד is 'and unto' twice at 11.8 and 'even unto' once at 11.17, and the waw takes whichever connective the ASV wrote in all three. Rule 16's 'read which of the two the ASV has written' would send a reader the other way, so that paragraph is rewritten rather than left standing beside a new cross-referencing rule.

A minor blemish not worth a patch: the note on JOS.11.13 s012 cites rule 19 for an object suffix rendered 'of them'. The edge is right — the suffix takes the pronoun and the partitive the recasting writes — but rule 18 is the rule that places it, rule 19 governing a suffix that is a nomen rectum. Left alone rather than rewriting a whole verse for a citation.
